claim: In the founding fireground study, experienced commanders showed option comparison in under 12% of 156 decision points and direct recognition of a typical situation and action in over 80% (26 commanders, mean 23 years). Retrospective interviews, one domain, authors coded the decision points.
agent_test: Not testable directly. Use as motivation only.

claim: Outside firefighting, coded expert decisions in sport are mostly simple match (60-81%), with diagnosis 13-28% and evaluating a course of action 3-24%. These use the RPD coding scheme, so the result is partly circular.
agent_test: Log what share of our agent's items a cheap first attempt solves and passes the check; compare with the 60-81% range as a sanity band only.
audit_note: Only a15 (a secondary report of Macquet 2020) gives the 60-81/13-28/3-24 figures; a16 is a single-goalkeeper case study (simple match 46%, simulation 34%, diagnosis 20%) that does not support them, and neither source mentions firefighting or circularity.

claim: In chess, quick judgement improves with skill: Elo accounted for 44% of the variance in position-evaluation error after 5 seconds (N=63, r=0.664; Chassy et al. 2023), and rank scores in 5-min blitz tournaments accounted for 64-81% of the variance in rank scores based on standard games (Burns 2004, as reported by Vidulich and Tsang 2026), which leaves 19-36% unexplained.
agent_test: Compare a one-shot fast answer with the full scaffold by difficulty bucket at equal tokens; the fast mode should capture most of the accuracy on easy items.
audit_note: Numbers check out (N=63, r=0.664, 44% of variance in evaluation error; Burns 64-81% of variance, via secondary report), but 'skill is largely fast pattern knowledge' is stronger than the sources: 44% leaves most error variance unexplained and blitz-standard overlap is a correlation, not proof of pattern knowledge.
claim_before_audit: In chess, skill is largely fast pattern knowledge: Elo explains 44% of error in a position-evaluation task (N=63, Chassy 2023), and rank in 5-min blitz explains 64-81% of rank in standard play (Burns, as reported by Vidulich and Tsang).

claim: Time pressure still hurts elite players, so recognition alone is not sufficient: grandmasters blunder more in blitz (t(19)=6.54, d=1.39, N=20; EBPM higher for 18 of 20), and Kasparov's rating-equivalent fell from 2750 to 2646 in simultaneous play.
agent_test: Cap thinking tokens on a hard-item set and measure the accuracy loss against a longer budget; the loss should be larger on hard than on easy items.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-01 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Extra deliberation helps both stronger and weaker chess players on hard positions, and the first move named is kept only 45% of the time overall (22% and 25% on hard positions). A secondary report of Calderwood et al. (1988) (3 class B vs 3 masters) said masters seemed immune to blitz; the original was not obtained and the larger study disagrees.
agent_test: Track how often the first harvested answer survives S4 to S8 and use it as the signal for when to search further. The 45% figure is a secondary report of Moxley 2012.

claim: Mode choice should depend on the gap between the best and second-best option and on position complexity: fast play does better when the evaluation gap is large, and worse when much search is needed.
agent_test: Gate on a cheap difficulty or margin signal (agreement between two short attempts, margin between top two candidates) and compare with a fixed budget at equal tokens.

claim: Strong chess play can be distilled into a network with no test-time search (270M transformer: puzzles 95.4%, tournament Elo 2299), yet search on top of a value network still adds a lot (Leela policy-only Elo 2292 vs 2858 with 400 MCTS simulations; puzzles 88.6% vs 99.6%). Note: the 93.5% puzzle score quoted from Monroe and Chalmers is their own re-run of the Ruoss model; Ruoss reports 95.4%. Keep them apart.
agent_test: Rows come from one paper (Ruoss 2024), checked against Table 1. Monroe and Chalmers (c11) report 93.5% for the same-size model on a different protocol. Test: fast answer vs fast answer plus tested search at equal tokens.

claim: Test-time search scales roughly with the log of simulations in a language-model chess player. Schultz et al. give +68 internal Elo at 100 simulations and, by the Table 1 rows read in order (inferred), about +290 to +340 at 500 to 2000 simulations. The '+300 with limited search' in the conclusion is a loose summary of that range, not a 100-simulation figure.
agent_test: Plot accuracy against attempts N on our agent; expect log-like gains and a plateau. Reconcile the +68 and +300 figures before citing.

claim: A human-like fast policy differs from the strongest policy: Maia predicts human moves at 46-52% accuracy while the best Stockfish version reaches at most 46%, and adding tree search to Maia lowers move-prediction accuracy.
agent_test: Not for the schema. Useful as a benchmark: a fast human-like policy is not the same object as the strongest search policy.
audit_note: Minor: Maia's lowest accuracy (46%, 1900-model on 1100 players) equals Stockfish's max, per-band accuracy is about 51-53%; the tree-search degradation is stated in Maia 1 (10 rollouts), not Maia-2, and the two papers are the same research line (overlapping authors).

claim: Language models trained only on chess text hold a board representation (probe accuracy 99.6%) and a latent player-skill estimate; adding a skill vector raised win rate up to 2.6 times.
agent_test: One paper counted twice (Karvonen 2024). No test for our agent; shows pattern knowledge can be stored without explicit rules.

claim: A chess network without search shows signs of look-ahead: a probe predicts the best move two turns ahead with 92% accuracy, but only in 22.5k puzzles kept from 900k and weaker when first and second target squares differ.
agent_test: Do not rely on it. Single paper, selective filtering.

claim: Prompting an LLM to reason by recognition-primed decision making raised care-seeking accuracy from 63.3% to 67.6% (OR 2.26, 13,500 assessments, 10 models). The gain is mostly on self-care cases (13.4% to 29.8%), only 2 emergency vignettes exist, and 88% of errors are over-triage. The nearest ablation compares RPD (67.6%) with a data-frame prompt without a simulation loop (66.7%, overlapping CIs), so the mental simulation step is not shown to add anything.
agent_test: Replicate on our own task family: RPD-style prompt (name the typical case, then act) vs default at equal tokens. Report per-category gains, not only the mean.

claim: Switching between a fast and a slow module on a simple stuck signal beat heavier single-mode agents: SwiftSage 84.7 vs 33.8-45.3 for baselines on 30 ScienceWorld task types, switching after 5 steps with zero reward.
agent_test: Implement the stuck rule (5 steps, no gain) as the trigger to deliberate and compare with always-slow at equal tokens. The baselines used different budgets, so equal-token checks are needed.

claim: Newer LLMs avoid the intuitive trap on cognitive reflection tasks (ChatGPT-4 96% correct vs 38% for humans, 0% intuitive errors), and blocking chain of thought only drops ChatGPT-4 from 95% to 88%, while GPT-3 rose from 5% to 28% with it.
agent_test: Measure plain answer vs long reasoning on easy items; if no gain, cap reasoning on those items.

claim: Learned switching between fast and slow reasoning can sharply cut slow reasoning: Thinkless reduces the use of long-chain thinking by 50-90% on Minerva Algebra, MATH-500 and GSM8K, with token savings smaller than that and a small accuracy drop on some benchmarks; and on Maze Navigation a tuned mix of fast and slow planning (System-1.x, x=0.5) gets 70.4% valid plans at 13.6 states vs 48.7% (System-1) and 37.2% (System-2).
agent_test: Use a router (code-based first) and compare with a fixed split at equal tokens.
audit_note: System-1.x numbers confirmed (Maze Navigation, 70.4% at 13.6 states vs 48.7 and 37.2). Thinkless abstract says it cuts the USE of long-chain thinking by 50-90%, not reasoning cost; Table 1 shows tokens falling only about 40-70% and some accuracy loss (e.g. MATH-500 0.861 to 0.795, Minerva 0.958 to 0.925 for the efficient row).
claim_before_audit: Learned switching between fast and slow reasoning can cut reasoning cost by 50-90% while keeping accuracy (Thinkless), and a tuned mix of fast and slow planning beats either extreme on one task (System-1.x: 70.4% valid plans at 13.6 states vs 48.7% and 37.2%).

claim: Experience-memory agents that recall solved situations can match learned policies: DiLu with 40 memory items matches RL trained for 600,000 episodes. Out-of-coverage check: in DiLu success fell from 70% to 35% when lanes and traffic density rose (10 scenarios each), so the match does not carry over fully; RL fell by 85%.
agent_test: Add a store of verified solved cases and test nearest-case retrieval before generating; measure transfer to unusual cases separately.

claim: RPD failure with novices and atypical cases has one measured case: in soccer referees (N=60) experts did equally well with intuitive and analytical style (.851 vs .835) while novices did better analytically (.690 vs .643). Qualitative studies (12 pharmacists, 11 residents) show a shift to analysis on atypical cases and premature closure in novices. The 'less than half' novice figure from Klein still has no source with N.
agent_test: Seed the agent with items outside the memory's coverage; the recognition mode must fall back to S1/S3 when no case matches. Needs a measured threshold.

claim: Take-the-first has about eight sport studies (scoping review), all from one research network or its students, with N=47 to 90 and 70% first-option use (Hepler and Feltz, N=72). One knowledge-free task (N=98) contradicted the TTF order. No failed replication in an expert sample was found; Johnson and Raab (2003) numbers and Klein et al. (1995) option counts remain unobtained.
agent_test: Open these papers before any claim; they decide whether generating more options hurts.

claim: On easy items a first pass is mostly enough and later reasoning wastes tokens: in over 92% of cases the first solution round of long-reasoning models was already correct, and trimming later rounds cut tokens 48.6% on MATH500 with accuracy kept. The best allocation shifts with difficulty (easy: sequential checking; medium-hard: search; hardest: little helps).
agent_test: Route by the pass rate of 2-3 quick attempts; compare tokens at equal budget on easy vs hard bins. No study with RPD framing tests a fast first attempt plus a code check at equal tokens.

claim: A fast first attempt plus a test-and-repair step does not reliably beat plain resampling at equal budget (0.97x to 1.05x in the cases quoted, up to +8% GPT-4 on APPS, up to +34% relative on competition-level problems). A verifier is what makes many cheap attempts pay; without one, voting and reward models plateau.
agent_test: Test fast-first plus code check against the same token budget in plain resampling, per difficulty bin.

claim: Switch signals that have been tested for leaving the cheap mode: agreement across sampled answers (Adaptive-Consistency: 3.3x fewer samples on average, accuracy drop below 0.1%), window unanimity (ESC: 33.8% to 84.2% fewer samples by task), and confidence weighting (over 40% fewer paths). A stuck counter was tested in SwiftSage (K13). Asking the model to re-check its own first answer without outside feedback does not work (GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 89.0 over two rounds).
agent_test: Use agreement of two to three short attempts as the default switch; add a stuck counter for multi-step tasks; do not use self-survival as the signal.
audit_note: All figures match (Adaptive-Consistency 3.3x avg, <0.1% drop; ESC 33.8-84.2%; CISC over 40%; Huang GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0). The SwiftSage stuck-counter reference (K13) was not among the listed sources and was not checked.

claim: No clean ablation of RPD step 3 (mentally simulate the single chosen option) exists. The closest, RPD vs data-frame prompting, shows no reliable extra gain, and external execution beats imagined execution (Chain of Code: 84 vs 72 for CoT on BIG-Bench Hard).
agent_test: Run a three-arm test: name typical case; name typical case plus simulate; name typical case plus real check.

claim: Independent replication of Klein's 80% outside RPD's own coding was not found. Non-fire RPD-framed studies (12 pharmacists, 11 residents, 39 ICU nurses) are qualitative and use RPD codes; a military study (N=225) measures beliefs, not decisions.
agent_test: Treat '80% recognition' as one study of 156 decisions plus sport studies coded with the same scheme.
